# Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding — Summary

**Paper:** "Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding" — Yaniv Leviathan, Matan Kalman, Yossi Matias (Google Research, Mountain View, CA, USA). Proceedings of the 40th International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2023), PMLR 202, 2023. arXiv:2211.17192v2 [cs.LG], 18 May 2023.

## Sources actually retrieved in this session

- `https://arxiv.org/pdf/2211.17192` — **FAILED.** `web_fetch` rejected it with the error: `web_fetch rejects non-textual content type 'application/pdf'.` (The tool cannot parse PDFs directly.)
- `https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.17192` — **succeeded** (HTML abstract page). Gave title, authors, abstract, metadata (ICML 2023 Oral), and links.
- `https://arxiv.org/html/2211.17192v2` — **succeeded** (arXiv LaTeXML HTML rendering). Gave the full text structure (TOC, abstract, Section 1, Section 2 with equations).
- `https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2211.17192` — **succeeded** (ar5iv HTML rendering). Gave the full body text including Section 2.1–2.3 and the equations.
- `https://r.jina.ai/https://arxiv.org/pdf/2211.17192` — **succeeded** (a text-extraction proxy that converts the PDF to Markdown). This was the most useful source: it returned the actual paper body including Algorithm 1 and the numbered equations of Section 3.

I then fetched the arXiv abstract page, the arXiv HTML version, the ar5iv HTML version, and finally a text-extraction proxy (`r.jina.ai`) that renders the PDF as plain text. The last one supplied the equations and algorithm verbatim.

Everything below is drawn from the content retrieved via those tool calls. Where the retrieved text was garbled by the HTML/Markdown conversion, I note the reconstruction.

---

## 1. Problem and core idea

Inference from large autoregressive models such as Transformers is slow: decoding `K` tokens takes `K` serial runs of the model. The paper introduces **speculative decoding**, an algorithm that samples from autoregressive models faster *without any change to the outputs*, by computing several tokens in parallel.

Two observations motivate it:
1. Hard language-modeling tasks often contain easier subtasks that can be approximated well by more efficient models.
2. Using speculative execution plus a novel sampling method, exact decoding from the large model can be made faster by running it in parallel on the outputs of the approximation models — potentially generating several tokens concurrently, and without changing the distribution.

The method accelerates off-the-shelf models with no retraining or architecture changes. On T5-XXL it gives a **2X–3X** acceleration versus the standard T5X implementation, with identical outputs.

The paper frames this as a generalization of *speculative execution* (branch prediction in processors) to the **stochastic** setting, where a task "might be needed" with some probability. Generations from a cheaper **approximation model** are used as speculative prefixes for the slower **target model**.

## 2. Setup and notation (Section 2.1, Overview)

- `M_p` — the **target model**, the one whose inference we want to accelerate.
- `p(x_t | x_{<t})` — the distribution obtained from `M_p` for a prefix `x_{<t}`.
- `M_q` — a more efficient **approximation model** for the same task.
- `q(x_t | x_{<t})` — the distribution obtained from `M_q` for a prefix `x_{<t}`.
- The paper writes `p(x)` for `p(x_t | x_{<t})` and `q(x)` for `q(x_t | x_{<t})` whenever the prefix is clear from context.
- `γ ∈ Z+` — the number of guesses/completions generated by `M_q` per iteration.

**The core idea (three steps):**
1. Use the more efficient model `M_q` to generate `γ ∈ Z+` completions (Section 3.5 discusses how to choose `γ` optimally).
2. Use the target model `M_p` to evaluate all of the guesses and their respective probabilities **in parallel**, accepting all those that can lead to an identical distribution.
3. Sample an additional token from an adjusted distribution to fix the first rejected guess, or to add an additional token if all guesses were accepted.

Consequently, each parallel run of `M_p` produces **at least one** new token (so the number of serial runs of the target model can never, even in the worst case, exceed that of simple autoregressive decoding), but it can potentially generate many new tokens, **up to `γ + 1`**, depending on how well `M_q` approximates `M_p`.

## 3. Standardized sampling (Section 2.2)

Sampling methods such as argmax, top-k, nucleus, and temperature scaling are usually treated differently at the logits level, but they can all be cast into standard sampling from an adjusted probability distribution. For example, argmax sampling is equivalent to zeroing out the non-max elements of the distribution and normalizing. The paper therefore deals only with standard sampling from a probability distribution, and assumes `p(x)` and `q(x)` are the distributions from `M_p` and `M_q` respectively, **adjusted for the sampling method**.

## 4. Speculative sampling (Section 2.3) — the key mechanism

To sample `x ∼ p(x)`, the algorithm instead samples `x ∼ q(x)` and applies this acceptance/rejection rule:

- **Keep** the sample if `q(x) ≤ p(x)`.
- If `q(x) > p(x)`, **reject** the sample with probability `1 − p(x)/q(x)`, and in that case sample `x` again from the adjusted distribution

  `p'(x) = norm(max(0, p(x) − q(x)))`

The paper states it is easy to show (Appendix A.1) that for **any** distributions `p(x)` and `q(x)`, a token `x` sampled this way satisfies `x ∼ p(x)` — i.e. the output distribution is exactly that of the target model.

**Two-token illustration from the paper:** given the distribution `q(x)` obtained by running `M_q` on a conditioning prefix, sample a token `x_1 ∼ q(x)`. Then compute the distribution `p(x)` by running `M_p` on the prefix, while *in parallel* speculatively computing the distribution of the next token `x_2` by running `M_p` on `prefix + [x_1]`. Once both computations complete: if `x_1` is rejected, discard the computation of `x_2` and re-sample `x_1` from the adjusted distribution; if `x_1` is accepted, keep both tokens.

### Algorithm 1 — `SpeculativeDecodingStep`

Inputs: `M_p`, `M_q`, `prefix`.

1. **Sample `γ` guesses `x_1, …, x_γ` from `M_q` autoregressively.**
   ```
   for i = 1 to γ do
       q_i(x) ← M_q(prefix + [x_1, …, x_{i−1}])
       x_i ∼ q_i(x)
   end for
   ```
2. **Run `M_p` in parallel.**
   ```
   p_1(x), …, p_{γ+1}(x) ← M_p(prefix), …, M_p(prefix + [x_1, …, x_γ])
   ```
3. **Determine the number of accepted guesses `n`.**
   ```
   r_1 ∼ U(0,1), …, r_γ ∼ U(0,1)
   n ← min( { i − 1 | 1 ≤ i ≤ γ, r_i > p_i(x)/q_i(x) } ∪ { γ } )
   ```
4. **Adjust the distribution from `M_p` if needed.**
   ```
   p'(x) ← p_{n+1}(x)
   if n < γ then
       p'(x) ← norm(max(0, p_{n+1}(x) − q_{n+1}(x)))
   end if
   ```
5. **Return one token from `M_p`, and `n` tokens from `M_q`.**
   ```
   t ∼ p'(x)
   return prefix + [x_1, …, x_n, t]
   ```

So each iteration emits `n` accepted guesses from `M_q` plus exactly one token `t` drawn from the target model's (possibly adjusted) distribution — guaranteeing at least one token per target-model run.

## 5. Analysis (Section 3) — the equations

### 5.1 Number of generated tokens (Section 3.1)

**Definition 3.1.** The **acceptance rate** `β_{x<t}`, given a prefix `x_{<t}`, is the probability of accepting `x_t ∼ q(x_t | x_{<t})` by speculative sampling.

`E(β)` is a natural measure of how well `M_q` approximates `M_p`. Under the simplifying assumption that the `β`s are i.i.d., with `α = E(β)`, the number of tokens produced by a single run of Algorithm 1 is a **capped geometric variable** with success probability `1 − α` and cap `γ + 1`. The expected number of tokens generated satisfies **Equation (1)**:

```
E(# generated tokens) = (1 − α^{γ+1}) / (1 − α)          (1)
```

(Figure 2 in the paper plots this expected number of tokens as a function of `α` for various `γ`.)

### 5.2 Calculating `α` (Section 3.2)

**Definition 3.2.** A divergence `D_LK` is defined as

```
D_LK(p, q) = Σ_x |p(x) − M(x)| = Σ_x |q(x) − M(x)|,   where M(x) = (p(x) + q(x)) / 2
```

**Lemma 3.3.**
```
D_LK(p, q) = 1 − Σ_x min(p(x), q(x))
```
Proof sketch (as given): `D_LK(p,q) = Σ_x |p(x) − M(x)| = Σ_x |p − q|/2 = 1 − Σ_x (p + q − |p − q|)/2 = 1 − Σ_x min(p(x), q(x))`.

**Corollary 3.4.** `D_LK(p, q)` is a symmetric divergence in `[0, 1]`; `D_LK(p, q) = 0 ⟺ p = q`; `D_LK(p, q) = 1 ⟺ p` and `q` have disjoint support.

**Theorem 3.5.**
```
β = 1 − D_LK(p, q)
```
Proof sketch: `β = E_{x∼q(x)}[ 1 if q(x) ≤ p(x); p(x)/q(x) if q(x) > p(x) ] = E_{x∼q(x)} min(1, p(x)/q(x)) = Σ_x min(p(x), q(x))`.

**Corollary 3.6.**
```
α = 1 − E(D_LK(p, q)) = E(min(p, q))
```

### 5.3 Walltime improvement (Section 3.3)

With the i.i.d. assumption, the algorithm reduces the number of calls to the target model by a factor of `(1 − α^{γ+1}) / (1 − α)`. The analysis assumes enough compute resources to support the increased concurrency, and specifically that `γ + 1` concurrent evaluations of `M_p` can run in parallel without increasing walltime.

**Definition 3.7.** The **cost coefficient** `c` is the ratio between the time for a single run of `M_q` and the time for a single run of `M_p`. Unlike `α` (an intrinsic property of the models and task), `c` depends on hardware configuration and software implementation details. In the paper's experiments, where `M_q` is typically a couple of orders of magnitude smaller than `M_p`, `c` was always less than `0.05` and often negligibly close to `0`.

**Theorem 3.8.** The expected improvement factor in total walltime by Algorithm 1 is

```
(1 − α^{γ+1}) / ( (1 − α)(γc + 1) )
```

Proof sketch: denote the cost of a single step of `M_p` by `T`. Each run of Algorithm 1 costs `Tcγ + T` (running `M_q` `γ` times and `M_p` once) and produces `(1 − α^{γ+1})/(1 − α)` tokens on average. So the expected cost per token is `((cγ + 1)(1 − α) / (1 − α^{γ+1})) T`, versus `T` for standard decoding. The theorem assumes long enough generations (the improvement factor is capped by the number of generated tokens, since `M_p` runs at least once).

**Corollary 3.9.** If `α > c`, there exists `γ` for which an improvement is obtained, and the improvement factor is at least

```
(1 + α) / (1 + c)
```

Proof sketch: if an improvement holds for `γ`, it also holds for any `0 < γ* < γ`, so evaluate Theorem 3.8 at `γ = 1`: `(1 − α²)/((1 − α)(c + 1)) = (1 + α)/(1 + c)`.

### 5.4 Number of arithmetic operations (Section 3.4)

Algorithm 1 does `γ + 1` runs of `M_p` in parallel, so concurrent arithmetic operations grow by a factor of `γ + 1`. Since it produces at most `γ + 1` tokens per run, the *total* number of arithmetic operations may be higher than standard decoding. When a guess from `M_q` is accepted, the increased concurrency is "free" and the total number of operations is not increased (neglecting the cost of `M_q`); when a guess is rejected, computation is wasted.

**Definition 3.10.** Let `ĉ` be the ratio of arithmetic operations per token of the approximation model `M_q` to that of the target model `M_p`.

**Theorem 3.11.** The expected factor of increase in the number of total operations of Algorithm 1 is

```
(1 − α)(γĉ + γ + 1) / (1 − α^{γ+1})
```

Proof sketch: let `T̂` be the number of arithmetic operations of a standard decoding baseline per token (one run of `M_p`). One iteration of Algorithm 1 costs `T̂ĉγ + T̂(γ + 1)` operations (`γ` runs of `M_q` and `γ + 1` parallel runs of `M_p`). Dividing by the expected number of tokens produced (Equation 1) and by `T̂` gives the result. If `α` is low, the increase in arithmetic operations is high, and vice versa. For Transformer decoders, the total number of arithmetic operations of Algorithm 1 (not counting `M_q` runs) can be bounded from above by a single run of a same-size Transformer **encoder**.

Unlike total arithmetic operations, total **memory accesses** can go down: the target model's weights and KV cache can be read once per execution of Algorithm 1, so the number of memory accesses for reading them shrinks by a factor of `(1 − α^{γ+1})/(1 − α)`, per Equation (1).

### 5.5 Choosing `γ` (Section 3.5)

Given `c` and `α` and assuming enough compute resources, the optimal `γ` maximizes the walltime improvement of Theorem 3.8, `(1 − α^{γ+1}) / ((1 − α)(γc + 1))`. Since `γ` is an integer it can be found numerically (Figure 3 plots optimal `γ` as a function of `α` for various `c`).

Table 1 (assuming `c = ĉ = 0`) illustrates the trade-off between inference speed and total arithmetic operations:

| α | γ | Operations | Speed |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.6 | 2 | 1.53X | 1.96X |
| 0.7 | 3 | 1.58X | 2.53X |
| 0.8 | 2 | 1.23X | 2.44X |
| 0.8 | 5 | 1.63X | 3.69X |
| 0.9 | 2 | 1.11X | 2.71X |
| 0.9 | 10 | 1.60X | 6.86X |

Because the `β`s are not constant, further improvement could come from predicting `β` and varying `γ` during the run. With an oracle for `γ`, `E(# generated tokens) = 1/(1 − α)`; for typical `c` and `α` and unbounded compute, the enhanced walltime improvement factor could be up to ~60% higher than with a fixed `γ`. The paper leaves this to future work.

### 5.6 Approximation models (Section 3.6)

Speculative sampling — and therefore speculative decoding — guarantees an identical output distribution for **any** choice of approximation model `M_q`, without restriction (Appendix A.1). In the experiments the authors mostly tested existing off-the-shelf smaller Transformers as approximation models, of the same architecture as the target models and using the same probability standardization. In that setup, choosing `M_q` to be around **two orders of magnitude smaller** than `M_p` usually performed best, balancing `α` and `c` (Theorem 3.8).

## 6. Experiments and results (as reported in the retrieved text)

- Tasks/model sizes analyzed: unconditional generation from a 97M-parameter GPT-like model trained on lm1b; English-to-German translation and news-article summarization with an 11B-parameter T5-XXL model; and a dialog task with a 137B-parameter LaMDA model.
- Walltime comparison for T5-XXL against the robust T5X implementation showed an out-of-the-box latency improvement of **2X–3X**, without any change to the outputs.
- Figure 1 example: a 38-token sentence was generated with only **9 serial runs** of the larger target model (97M parameters) thanks to a smaller, more efficient approximation model (6M parameters), while the probability of generating it is unchanged. In the first line of that figure the target model was run only once and 5 tokens were generated.

## 7. Contributions (as stated by the paper)

1. A generalization of speculative execution to the stochastic setting, with a novel sampling method called **speculative sampling**.
2. A decoding mechanism called **speculative decoding** that accelerates decoding from autoregressive models without any change to model architectures, training regimes, or output distributions.
